source_text: Non tamen nos moueat aut turbet multorum nimia et abrupta perfidia, sed potius fidem nostram praenuntiatae rei ueritate corroboret. ut quidam tales esse coeperunt, quia haec ante praedicta sunt, ita ceteri fratres ab eiusmodi caueant, quia et haec ante praedicta sunt instruente Domino et dicente: uos autem cauete, ecce praedixi uobis omnia. uitate quaeso uos eiusmodi homines et a latere adque auribus uestris perniciosa conloquia uelut contagium mortis arcete, sicut scriptum est: saepi aures tuas spinis et noli audire linguam nequam. et iterum: conrumpunt ingenia bona confabulationes. pessimae. docet Dominus et admonet a talibus recedendum: caeci sunt, inquit, duces caecorum. caecus autem caecum ducens simul in foueam cadent. auersandus. est talis adque fugiendus quisque fuerit ab ecclesia separatus. peruersus est huiusmodi et peccat et est a semet ipso damnatus. an esse sibi cum Christo uidetur qui aduersum sacerdotes Christi facit, qui se a cleri eius et plebis societate secernit? arma ille contra ecclesiam portat, contra Dei dispositionem repugnat. hostis altaris, aduersus sacrificium Christi rebellis, pro fide perfidus, pro religione sacrilegus, inobsequens seruus, filius impius, frater inimicus contemptis episcopis et Dei sacerdotibus derelictis constituere audet aliud altare, precem alteram inlicitis uocibus facere, dominicae hostiae ueritatem per falsa sacrificia profanare, nec scire quoniam qui contra ordinationem Dei nititur ob temeritatis audaciam diuina animaduersione punitur.
thought_title: Avoid and flee those separated from the Church
orientation: Cyprian is addressing the faithful, urging them not to be disturbed by the faithlessness of many but to be strengthened by the fact that such defections were foretold, and to avoid those who have separated from the Church.
pass_a_gloss: But let not the excessive and abrupt faithlessness of many move us or disturb us, but rather let it strengthen our faith by the truth of the thing foretold. As certain ones began to be such, because these things were foretold beforehand, so let the rest of the brothers beware of men of this kind, because these things also were foretold beforehand, with the Lord instructing and saying: but you, beware; behold, I have foretold all things to you. Avoid, I beg you, men of this kind, and keep away from your side and from your ears their pernicious conversations as the contagion of death, as it is written: fence your ears with thorns and do not listen to a wicked tongue. And again: evil conversations corrupt good minds. The Lord teaches and warns that one must withdraw from such men: they are blind, he says, leaders of the blind. But a blind man leading a blind man will fall into a pit together. Such a one is to be turned away from and fled, whoever has been separated from the Church. A man of this kind is perverse and sins and is condemned by himself. Or does he seem to himself to be with Christ, who acts against the priests of Christ, who separates himself from the society of his clergy and people? He bears arms against the Church, he fights against God's ordering. An enemy of the altar, a rebel against the sacrifice of Christ, faithless in place of faith, sacrilegious in place of religion, a disobedient servant, an impious son, an enemy brother, with the bishops despised and the priests of God abandoned, he dares to set up another altar, to make another prayer with unlawful words, to profane the truth of the Lord's victim through false sacrifices, and not to know that whoever strives against God's ordinance is punished by divine vengeance for the boldness of his rashness.

choices.why: Keeps the double object of separation literally, showing both physical and auditory avoidance.

choices.why: Uses the glossary term 'altar' and keeps the genitive force of hostility toward the altar.

choices.why: Keeps 'hostia' as 'victim' (sacrificial offering) and the genitive 'dominicae' as 'of the Lord,' matching the sacrificial context.

pass_b_english: But let the excessive and abrupt faithlessness of many not move or disturb us. Instead, let it strengthen our faith by the truth of the thing foretold. Just as certain people have begun to be this way because these things were predicted beforehand, so let the rest of the brethren beware of such people, because these things too were predicted beforehand, with the Lord instructing and saying: "But you, beware; behold, I have foretold everything to you" (Mark 13:23). I beg you, avoid people of this kind, and keep their destructive conversations away from your side and from your ears like the contagion of death, as it is written: "Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue" (Sirach 28:24). And again: "Bad conversations corrupt good minds" (1 Corinthians 15:33). The Lord teaches and warns that we must withdraw from such people. "They are blind," he says, "leaders of the blind. And if a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit" (Matthew 15:14). Whoever has been separated from the Church is to be turned away from and fled. Such a person is perverse, and he sins, and he is condemned by himself. Does someone who acts against the priests of Christ, who cuts himself off from the fellowship of his clergy and people, think that he is with Christ? He bears arms against the Church; he fights against God's ordering. He is an enemy of the altar, a rebel against the sacrifice of Christ, faithless in place of faith, sacrilegious in place of religion, a disobedient servant, an impious son, a hostile brother. Despising the bishops and abandoning the priests of God, he dares to set up another altar, to make another prayer with unlawful words, to profane the truth of the Lord's victim through false sacrifices, and does not know that whoever strives against God's ordinance is punished by divine judgment for the audacity of his rashness.

problems.why: 'Nec scire' is an exclamation of indignant surprise ('and does he not know...?'), not a statement of fact. The English flattens this to mere ignorance.
problems.ruling: 'nec scire quoniam...' continues the indignant rhetorical question 'an esse sibi...uidetur'; it means 'and does he not know that...'

fixed: Changed 'and he does not know' to 'and does he not know' to render 'nec scire' as an indignant rhetorical question rather than a flat statement of ignorance.

problems.source_quote: et iterum: conrumpunt ingenia bona confabulationes. pessimae.
problems.why: The Latin source quotes Sirach 28:24 immediately before with 'sicut scriptum est', then introduces this with 'et iterum' ('and again'), indicating the same book. The quote 'corrupt good minds' matches Sirach, not 1 Cor 15:33 (which has 'evil communications corrupt good manners' in KJV or similar). The citation to 1 Corinthians is wrong.

problems.quote: "Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue" (Sirach 28:24)
problems.source_quote: saepi aures tuas spinis et noli audire linguam nequam
problems.ruling: Vulgate Sirach 28:28 reads 'saepi aures tuas spinis...'; verse 28:24 differs. Reference is wrong.

problems.why: The Latin 'nec scire' is an indirect statement dependent on the preceding series of infinitives (audet... facere... profanare... nec scire), meaning 'nor does he know' or 'and he does not know.' The English 'and does he not know' changes this to a rhetorical question, which alters the syntax and force. The Latin states he dares these things 'and does not know'—a statement of fact, not a question.
problems.ruling: 'nec scire' continues infinitives after 'audet'; it is declarative 'nor does he know,' not the rhetorical question 'does he not know.'

edits.old: "Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue" (Sirach 28:24)
edits.new: "Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue" (Sirach 28:28)

fixed: Changed 'and does he not know' to 'and does not know' because the Latin 'nec scire' is an indirect statement, not a rhetorical question.
Changed Sirach 28:24 to Sirach 28:28 for 'Fence your ears with thorns...' per the Vulgate/LXX numbering.
Changed 1 Corinthians 15:33 to Sirach 28:25 for 'Bad conversations corrupt good minds' because the source introduces it with 'et iterum' after a Sirach quotation.

problems.why: The verse is from 1 Corinthians 15:33, not Sirach. Cyprian quotes Paul's famous warning, not Sirach.

problems.source_quote: saepi aures tuas spinis et noli audire linguam nequam
problems.why: The verse is from Sirach 28:24 (Vulgate numbering), not 28:28. The Vulgate has different verse numbering here.
problems.ruling: Source 'saepi aures tuas spinis' is Sirach 28:24 in Vulgate, not 28:28; wrong scripture reference misleads reader.

edits.old: "Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue" (Sirach 28:28)
edits.new: "Fence your ears with thorns, and do not listen to a wicked tongue" (Sirach 28:24)

fixed: Changed Sirach 28:25 to 1 Corinthians 15:33: the source 'conrumpunt ingenia bona confabulationes pessimae' is Paul's quotation in 1 Corinthians 15:33, not Sirach.
Changed Sirach 28:28 to Sirach 28:24: the Vulgate numbering for 'saepi aures tuas spinis et noli audire linguam nequam' is Sirach 28:24.

last_rejected.why: Cyprian quotes this as Scripture but the source lacks Pauline attribution; the work brief shows no Paul speaker in section 17. The English adds a false citation.
last_rejected.fix: Remove '(1 Corinthians 15:33)' or mark as unattributed Scripture quotation.
last_rejected.ruling: 1 Cor 15:33 is the correct source of 'conrumpunt ingenia bona confabulationes pessimae'; adding the reference is standard, not a false citation.

last_rejected.quote: The Lord teaches and warns that we must withdraw from such people. "They are blind," he says
last_rejected.source_quote: docet Dominus et admonet a talibus recedendum: caeci sunt, inquit, duces caecorum
last_rejected.why: The English makes the blind leaders quote follow as if the Lord speaks it, but 'inquit' introduces a separate saying; the Lord's teaching precedes, this is a distinct quotation.
last_rejected.fix: The Lord teaches and warns that we must withdraw from such people. For it is said: "They are blind..."
last_rejected.ruling: 'docet Dominus...caeci sunt, inquit' naturally reads as the Lord speaking; 'inquit' introduces the Lord's quoted words, not a separate speaker.

last_rejected.why: 'A semet ipso' means 'by himself' in the sense of acting on his own initiative/automatically, not self-condemnation. The person is condemned on his own account/self-acting, not that he pronounces judgment on himself.
last_rejected.fix: he stands condemned on his own account
last_rejected.ruling: 'a semet ipso damnatus' = 'condemned by himself'; self-condemnation is a standard patristic reading, within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: to make another prayer with unlawful words
last_rejected.why: 'Precem' here means prayer in the liturgical sense of a set prayer/rite, not merely 'prayer.' The context is rival liturgical practice (another altar, false sacrifices).
last_rejected.fix: to perform another rite with unlawful words
last_rejected.ruling: 'prayer' is the normal meaning of 'precem'; liturgical nuance is contextually implied but 'prayer' is not a mistranslation.
